To infect means to enter something living and cause harm by spreading inside it. Think of it as an unwanted, harmful thing getting into a body — or anything else — and then doing damage from the inside out.

The key idea is not just presence, but transmission and spread. Something harmful passes from one source into a new host and begins to take hold.

This is the primary and most literal meaning. When a germ — a virus, bacterium, fungus, or parasite — enters a living body (human, animal, or plant) and begins to cause disease or illness, we say it infects that body.

Examples:

  • The flu virus infected hundreds of people in the village.
  • Bacteria can infect an open wound if you don't clean it.
  • Mosquitoes infect humans with malaria when they bite.
  • The fungus infected the crops and destroyed the entire harvest.

Notice who or what is doing the infecting: it's always the harmful agent — the germ, the parasite, the mosquito carrying a disease. The person, animal, or plant is on the receiving end. They get infected.

A person can also infect another person:

  • She had a cold and infected her whole family.
  • He didn't know he was sick, but he infected several colleagues at work.

Here, the person themselves becomes the carrier — the source — and passes the harmful microorganism on to someone else.

Important nuance: Something can infect a specific part of the body too, not just the whole body:

  • The bacteria infected his lungs.
  • The virus infected her bloodstream.
  • The cut became infected (meaning bacteria entered and began causing harm in that wound).

In computing, infect is used when malicious software — a virus, malware, or a worm — gets into a computer, phone, file, or entire network and begins to damage or disrupt it. This meaning is directly borrowed from biology because the behaviour is so similar: something harmful enters, spreads, and causes damage.

Examples:

  • The malware infected thousands of computers worldwide.
  • Clicking that link infected the entire company's network.
  • The virus infected every file on his hard drive.
Meaning 3 — The Figurative Sense (Ideas, Emotions, Attitudes)

This is where the word becomes truly powerful and rich. Infect can be used metaphorically to describe how a feeling, attitude, idea, or mood spreads from one person (or source) to others, often taking hold without much resistance — just like a biological infection.

In most figurative uses, infect carries a negative or unwanted tone. Something undesirable spreads to people who didn't ask for it:

  • His constant negativity infected the entire team's morale.
  • Fear infected the crowd and people started to panic.
  • The culture of dishonesty in that company infected even the most ethical employees over time.
  • Her anxiety infected everyone around her.

However — and this is an important nuance — "infect" can occasionally be used figuratively in a positive way, usually to describe something joyful or energetic that spreads irresistibly. When used positively, there is often a sense of pleasant surprise or delight at how unstoppably the feeling spreads:

  • His laughter infected the whole room and soon everyone was giggling.
  • Her enthusiasm for the project infected every single person on the team.
  • The lead dancer's energy infected the entire audience.

Even in these positive cases, the structure of the meaning stays the same: something originates in one source and spreads outward into others, taking hold whether they planned for it or not.
The Three Things Always Present When "Infect" Is Used

No matter which sense of the word you encounter, three things are always true:

1. There is a source — the thing doing the infecting (a germ, a virus, a person, a feeling, malware).

2. There is a receiver — the thing being infected (a body, a computer, a crowd, a culture).

3. There is a spread — the harmful (or powerful) thing moves from the source into the receiver and establishes itself there.

If any of these three elements are missing, the word "infect" wouldn't quite fit.
What Can "Infect" Take as Its Object?

The word is flexible. Here is a sense of all that can be infected:

  • A person or animal: The virus infected him badly.
  • A body part: The bacteria infected her knee joint.
  • A plant or crop: Mildew infected the rose bushes.
  • A computer or digital system: The ransomware infected the hospital's servers.
  • A group of people: Fear infected the passengers on the plane.
  • A culture or institution: Corruption infected the government from the top down.
  • A mind or way of thinking: The propaganda infected the minds of an entire generation.

"Infect" is not a gentle word. It implies that the spreading happens without easy resistance and that the thing being infected is changed — often significantly — as a result. You don't merely touch something when you infect it. You get inside it and alter it.

This is what makes "infect" feel strong and serious even in casual use.

Since you'll encounter these constantly alongside "infect," knowing them helps complete the picture:

  • Infected (adjective/past tense): already harmed by an infection — an infected wound, an infected file.
  • Infection (noun): the process or result of infecting — a bacterial infection, an infection spreading through a city.
  • Infectious (adjective): capable of infecting; easily spread — an infectious disease, an infectious laugh.
  • Infective (adjective): relating to or capable of causing infection — used more in medical/technical contexts.
  • Disinfect (verb): the opposite — to remove or destroy infection-causing agents — to disinfect a surface.

To infect is to introduce something harmful into a host — whether a body, a computer, or even a social environment — causing it to be damaged, changed, or compromised from within. The word always carries the idea of transmission, of something spreading from a source into a new place and taking hold. In everyday life, you'll see it used in medicine, technology, and everyday speech to describe anything that spreads and takes root in an unwanted — or occasionally overwhelming — way.
